# Owner directives (highest priority; supersede roadmap/CI/portability wording)

1. **macOS only initially.** Apple Silicon, macOS 13+. No Linux or Windows code, CI jobs, runners, shims, packaging or portability work until the owner lifts this.
2. Keep platform code isolated behind `platform/` interfaces (clean seams only; no stubs or ports for other OSes).
3. CI/dev scripts target macOS only. Skip any roadmap item for Linux/Windows (M11, M12) and cross-platform CI matrices.

4. **Full Rust port, owner direction2026-10-14.** Stop the former C implementation queue. Port all first-party application/platform/UI/parser/raster/document/animation/MCP code and in-repo development/test tooling to Rust, then complete the existing product finish line. This supersedes the C17 language/build lock and the former two-implementation-worker ceiling. Use as many useful disjoint Luna codex exec workers as available allowance/resources permit; preserve one writer per module and coordinator-only shared integration. Existing subscription allowance only, no extra credits/API billing. Preserve the current C code, unfinished candidates and evidence as migration references; no delete/reset or false completion claim. macOS13+ AppleSilicon, MPL2, custom UI, owned source-preserving SVG/XML parser/rasterizer, minimal reviewed/pinned dependencies, and no GPL editor source remain locked. Broad UI/E2E at the final stage; focused correctness checks continue.
# Agent rules

Read [OWNER-DIRECTIVES.md](OWNER-DIRECTIVES.md) first. It overrides conflicting
roadmap and tooling text. Follow the active `work/WO-*.md`; inspect its allowed
and protected paths before editing. Keep each work order buildable, tested,
verified, and recorded in `STATE.md` and the ledgers.

## Platform and product locks

- Initial support is Apple Silicon macOS 13+. Do not add Linux/Windows code,
  shims, CI jobs, runners, packaging, or portability work.
- Keep platform implementations behind `platform/` interfaces; do not add
  stubs for unsupported operating systems.
- Rust for all first-party code is the active owner-approved migration target.
  MPL-2.0, minimal pinned dependencies, custom-drawn UI, and an owned SVG
  parser/rasterizer remain locked. Legacy C17 code is preserved as migration
  reference; do not resume old C implementation orders. See ADR-0022.
- Never read, fetch, or copy GPL SVG-editor source. Do not fetch external SVG
  resources from the application. Record provenance for external algorithms.

## Repository map

- `app/`: executable composition.
- `src/`: base, platform, XML/SVG, scene, raster, document, UI modules as added.
- `docs/research-r4/`: authoritative operating model and roadmap.
- `docs/research-r3/plan/`: architecture and coding guidance where r4 is silent.
- `docs/adr/`: accepted decisions; `work/`: immutable ready work orders.
- `tests/`: unit, property, fuzz, UI, and oracle tests as introduced.
- `bench/`: corpus metadata, generators, runners, and results.
- `artifacts/`: work-order evidence; `build/` and `.cache/` are generated.

## Commands

The commands below are the preserved legacy C workflow. Rust workspace/build
commands become authoritative only through their implementation orders.

- `./dev build`: configure and build Debug.
- `./dev test-fast`: run local Python tests and validate the ledger.
- `./dev verify`: run the Debug build and fast tests.
- `cmake --preset mac-release && cmake --build --preset mac-release`: Release.
- `python3 scripts/ledger.py validate ledger.jsonl`: validate work history.
- `python3 -m unittest`: run Python harness tests when present.
- `bench`, `fmt`, `lint`, `asan`, and `fuzz` become authoritative only when
  their work orders implement them; do not claim missing commands run.

## Engineering and safety

Use the contracts in `docs/CODING_STANDARD.md`: explicit ownership, pointer+length
slices, checked size arithmetic, bounded user input, no VLAs, and no unsafe
string functions. Preserve unknown SVG/XML source. Keep generated files in
ignored repo-local directories. Do not install system packages or touch sibling
directories. Add dependencies only through an ADR and pinned provenance record.

Never weaken frozen acceptance tests or oracles. Run commands named by the
active work order, then report exact evidence. Do not invent test or performance
results. Keep source files focused and under 800 lines; split cohesive modules
before they grow further.

## Rust migration execution

Follow `docs/product/rust-port-goal-and-plan.md` and ready Rust work orders.
Multiple Luna codex exec processes are authorized, with isolated current-source
worktrees and disjoint modules; coordinator alone changes shared manifests,
locks, interfaces and ledgers. Use Low for inventory/docs, Medium for routine
ports, High for parser/renderer/concurrency/unsafe FFI. Escalate only on a named
problem; use the existing subscription allowance and no purchased credits.
Preserve strict validation, original fixtures/assertions and byte-preserving
round trips. Rust ownership replaces manual C ownership conventions; bounded
inputs, checked arithmetic, safe cleanup and source limits still apply. Keep
unsafe operations behind documented platform/FFI boundaries.

# Scientific evidence for Vexel rendering and responsiveness

Date: 2026-10-14. Work order: WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01.
Requested skill: `science-paper-search`. This is a targeted literature review
for rendering, parsing resource bounds, and interaction latency within the
existing full Rust product goal. It does not establish performance gains or
complete the renderer, editor, native UI, or live MCP integration.

## Search and evidence

Used the free unauthenticated ScienceMadeReadable/OpenAlex route. The web tool
could not open its guide; the bundled standard-library helper fetched the
current guide successfully. All eight API requests returned HTTP200, including
five searches, one similarity expansion and one citation walk, plus the guide.
Requests were sequential and spaced beyond2.1seconds. No account, server
registration, credits, dependency, or private project information was submitted.

Queries searched GPU vector/path rasterization (semantic and exact terms),
bounded incremental XML, and input-feedback latency, then expanded the2016
scanline seed with similarity/citation queries. An exact inking-title search
checked publication versions. Raw timestamped request/response envelopes,
`query-log.json`, `screened-records.json`, `version-reconciliation.json` and
hashed primary PDFs/text extractions are in the work-order artifacts.

The index covers titles/abstracts, not full papers. This is not an exhaustive
survey or a ranking-based algorithm decision. Some exact-word results concerned
vectorization, neural generation or3D rendering and were excluded as different
tasks. Citation walking suggested silhouette texture magnification; that is
outside the present SVG editing scope. No external implementation was copied,
no GPL editor source was read, and code licenses were not established: any
future adoption needs separate provenance/dependency review.

## Relevant primary evidence

Full texts were obtained for the first five entries below; methods,
experimental setup, evaluation and limitations relevant to Vexel were examined,
rather than claiming every section was reviewed. The final entry remains a
retrieved abstract shortlist because its author endpoint failed TLS hostname
verification; certificate checks were retained.

| Paper | What the evidence supports | Limits for Vexel |
|---|---|---|
| [Nehab & Hoppe, Random-access rendering of general vector graphics (2008)](https://hhoppe.com/ravg.pdf) | Cell-local descriptions reduce work to spatially relevant primitives; extended cell regions support filtering. The paper explicitly discusses static-layout/re-encoding and unsupported-attribute limitations. | DirectX10/GeForce8800GTX, not AppleMetal. Include preprocessing, replicated storage, edit invalidation, thin strokes and corner quality in comparisons. |
| [Ganacim et al., Massively-parallel vector graphics (2014)](https://w3.impa.br/~diego/publications/GanEtAl14.pdf) | A shortcut-tree pipeline parallelizes preprocessing by segment and rendering by sample/pixel. Evaluations use a GTXTitan and report preprocessing separately from rendering. | Old GPU/hardware and selected vector illustrations. Raster timings alone do not establish editor latency, SVG fidelity or whole-frame rebuild cost. |
| [Konrad & Magniez, Validating XML Documents in the Streaming Model with External Memory (arXiv1012.3311)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.3311) | General DTD validation has space/pass trade-offs; the external-memory algorithm uses additional streams and passes. | The downloaded revision is2021; initial preprint2010, with later conference/journal versions. This is DTD validation, not our lexical source-preserving parser or editable DOM. It does not prove constant-memory editing. |
| [Ng et al., Designing for low-latency direct-touch input (UIST2012)](https://www.tactuallabs.com/papers/designingLowLatencyDirectTouchInputUIST12.pdf) | Ten right-handed participants compared direct-touch dragging delays on special low-latency hardware. The paper proposes immediate simple feedback followed by detailed visuals. | Touch demonstrator and perceptual discrimination, not macOS mouse/tablet productivity or application performance. Its low-millisecond observations are not universal acceptance thresholds. |
| [Annett et al., How Low Should We Go? (Graphics Interface2014)](https://webdocs.cs.ualberta.ca/~wfb/publications/C-2014-GI-Latency.pdf) | Writing/sketching with a custom stylus system produced different perceptual thresholds from simpler dragging. The first experiment uses12 participants and examines just-noticeable differences. | Perception differs from tolerance and task completion. The indexed2020 chapter is treated as a related version, not another replication. No blanket50ms product threshold follows. |
| [Li, Hou & Zhou, Efficient GPU path rendering using scanline rasterization (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1145/2980179.2982434) | Retrieved abstract describes boundary-fragment work and bulk interior spans. Retained as a candidate for later primary evaluation. | Full author PDF unavailable in this run. Reported speedups are not verified here or transferable to AppleSilicon. |

## Testable implementation directions

These are engineering inferences from the evidence, not measured Vexel results.

1. **Retain spatially local rendering and bounded caching.** Keep source/vector
   data editable and preserved. Evaluate coarse tile/cell culling and local
   invalidation; measure overlap amplification and cache metadata as well as
   pixels. Compare against the owned CPU renderer before choosing a Metal path.
2. **Include every stage in animation costs.** Measure decoding, path expansion,
   spatial preprocessing, invalidation, rendering and presentation separately
   and together. Use both static pan/zoom and changing artwork/timeline input;
   caching a static illustration cannot establish animated-frame performance.
3. **Separate progress from validation.** A partial preview must not certify an
   unvalidated document. Keep bounded per-step work, cancellation and explicit
   storage errors; charge actual reserved token/table capacity. Streaming
   visitors and retained editable models have different memory requirements.
4. **Measure feedback by task and input.** Record input-to-first-visible-feedback
   and input-to-final-frame for drawing, dragging/nodes, pan/zoom, playback and
   live MCP transactions. Fast previews must converge to faithful output and
   visibly report transaction/progress/cancel state, preserving undo integrity.
5. **Preserve existing product budgets.** ADR0018’s100MB/2second first-content,
   <100ms owner-thread pause and p95<33ms pan/zoom targets remain unchanged.
   Later work orders must name AppleSilicon hardware/OS/build, corpus hashes,
   cold/warm protocol, repeated p50/p95/worst samples and memory/quality results.
   Record end-to-end latency separately from renderer duration. No new broad
   UI/performance suite ran during this research.

## Gaps and next evidence

AppleMetal equivalence, full SVG clips/masks/text/effects, dynamic source editing,
MCP transaction observability and representative-user measurements remain open.
The review does not select an external renderer or retire the owned parser.
Native animation authoring and Rust/AppKit integration still follow the full
product plan. Comprehensive UI/E2E, fidelity, performance, accessibility,
recovery, packaged-release and authentic recorded demos remain final gates.

artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:20:                                                  We study the problem of validating XML documents of size N against general DTDs in the context
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:21:                                              of streaming algorithms. The starting point of this work is a well-known space lower bound. There are
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:22:                                              XML documents and DTDs for which p-pass streaming algorithms require Ω(N/p) space.
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:26:                                                  An important intermediate step of this algorithm is the computation of the First-Child-Next-Sibling
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:28:                                              dently, and we also provide memory efficient streaming algorithms for decoding an XML document given
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:31:                                              external memory can be done with sublinear memory. There is a one-pass algorithm using O( N log N )
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:32:                                              space, and a bidirectional two-pass algorithm using O(log2 N ) space performing this task.
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:36:                                        The area of streaming algorithms has experienced tremendous growth over the last decade in many appli-
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:37:                                        cations. Streaming algorithms sequentially scan the whole input piece by piece in one pass, or in a small
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:38:                                        number of passes (i.e., they do not have random access to the input), while using sublinear memory space,
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:39:                                        ideally polylogarithmic in the size of the input. The design of streaming algorithms is motivated by the ex-
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:40:                                        plosion in the size of the data that algorithms are called upon to process in everyday real-time applications.
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:43:                                        was one of the first applications of this kind of algorithm.

                                                                                            Abstract
                                                  We study the problem of validating XML documents of size N against general DTDs in the context
                                              of streaming algorithms. The starting point of this work is a well-known space lower bound. There are
                                              XML documents and DTDs for which p-pass streaming algorithms require Ω(N/p) space.
                                                  We show that when allowing access to external memory, there is a deterministic streaming algo-
                                              rithm that solves this problem with memory space O(log2 N ), a constant number of auxiliary read/write
                                              streams, and O(log N ) total number of passes on the XML document and auxiliary streams.
                                                  An important intermediate step of this algorithm is the computation of the First-Child-Next-Sibling
                                              (FCNS) encoding of the initial XML document in a streaming fashion. We study this problem indepen-
                                              dently, and we also provide memory efficient streaming algorithms for decoding an XML document given
                                              in its FCNS encoding.
                                                  Furthermore, validating XML documents encoding binary trees in the usual streaming model√ without
                                              external memory can be done with sublinear memory. There is a one-pass algorithm using O( N log N )
                                              space, and a bidirectional two-pass algorithm using O(log2 N ) space performing this task.


                                        1    Introduction
                                        The area of streaming algorithms has experienced tremendous growth over the last decade in many appli-
                                        cations. Streaming algorithms sequentially scan the whole input piece by piece in one pass, or in a small
                                        number of passes (i.e., they do not have random access to the input), while using sublinear memory space,
                                        ideally polylogarithmic in the size of the input. The design of streaming algorithms is motivated by the ex-
                                        plosion in the size of the data that algorithms are called upon to process in everyday real-time applications.
                                        Examples of such applications occur in bioinformatics for genome decoding, in Web databases for the search
                                        of documents, or in network monitoring. The analysis of Internet traffic [1], in which traffic logs are queried,
                                        was one of the first applications of this kind of algorithm.
                                            There are various extensions of this basic streaming model. One of them gives the streaming algorithm
                                        access to an external memory consisting of several read/write streams [9, 11, 7]. Then the streaming algorithm
                                        is also relaxed to perform multiple passes in any direction over the input stream and the auxiliary streams.

 In most of the applications, the number of auxiliary streams is constant and the total number of passes is
logarithmic in the input size.
    Verifying properties or evaluating queries of massive databases is an active and challenging topic. For
relational algebra queries against relational databases, the situation is quite clear. There are bidirectional
O(log N )-pass deterministic streaming algorithms with constant memory space and a constant number of
auxiliary streams [8]. Moreover, the logarithmic number of passes is a necessary condition in order to keep
the memory space sublinear, even if randomization is allowed. The latter was initially stated for one-sided
error [8] and then extended to two-sided error [4, 3].
    In the context of data exchange, especially on the Web, Extended Markup Language (XML) is emerging
as the standard, and is currently drawing much attention in data management research. Only few is known on
XML query processing when only streaming access is allowed to the XML document. For evaluating XQuery
and XPath queries against XML documents of size N , only the lower bound has been extended [8, 4, 3],
meaning that Ω(log N ) passes are necessary. For the upper bound, only simple refinements of the direct
algorithm are known: no auxiliary stream, one pass and linear memory in the height of the XML document,
which in the worst case is as large as N .
    This paper considers the problem of validating XML documents against a given Document Type Definition
(DTD) in a streaming fashion without restrictions on the DTD. Prior works on that topic [18, 17] essentially
try to characterize those DTDs for which validity can be checked by a finite-state automaton, that is a one-
pass deterministic streaming algorithm with constant memory. Concerning arbitrary DTDs, two approaches
have been considered in [18]. The first one leads to an algorithm with memory space linear in the height
of the XML document [18]. The second one consists in constructing a refined DTD of at most quadratic
size, which defines a similar family of tree documents as the original one, and against which validation can
be done with constant space. Nonetheless, for an existing document and DTD, the later requires that both,
documents and DTD, are converted before validation.
    One of the obstacles prior works had to cope with was to check well-formedness of XML documents, that
is every opening tag matches its same-level closing tag. Due to the past work of [14], we can now perform
such a verification with a constant-pass randomized streaming  √ algorithm with sublinear memory space and
no auxiliary streams. In one-pass the memory space is O( N log N ), and collapses to O(log2 N ) with an
additional pass in reverse direction.
    The starting point of this work is the fact that checking validity is hard without auxiliary streams.
There are DTDs defining ternary XML documents for which any p-pass bidirectional randomized streaming
algorithm requires Ω(N/p) space. This lower bound comes from encoding a well known communication
complexity problem, Set-Disjointness, as an XML validity problem. This lower bound should be well-known,
however we are not aware of a complete proof in the literature. In [10], a similar approach using ternary
trees with a reduction to Set-Disjointness is used for proving lower bounds for queries. For the sake of
completeness we provide a proof in Appendix A.
    An XML document is valid against a DTD if for each node, the sequence of the labels of their children
fulfills a regular expression defined in the DTD. For the case of XML documents encoding binary trees,
we present in Section 3 two deterministic streaming algorithms for checking validity with sublinear space.
As a consequence, the presence of nodes of degree at least 3 is indeed a necessary condition for the linear

    "abstract": "Edge aliasing continues to be one of the most prominent problems in real-time graphics, e.g., in games. We present a novel algorithm that uses shared memory between the GPU and the CPU so that these two units can work in concert to solve the edge aliasing problem rapidly. Our system renders the scene as usual on the GPU with one sample per pixel. At the same time, our novel edge aliasing algorithm is executed asynchronously on the CPU. First, a sparse set of important pixels is created. This set may include pixels with geometric silhouette edges, discontinuities in the frame buffer, and pixels/polygons under user-guided artistic control. After that, the CPU runs our sparse rasterizer and fragment shader, which is parallel and SIMD:ified, and directly accesses shared resources (e.g., render targets created by the GPU). Our system can render a scene with shadow mapping with adaptive anti-aliasing with 16 samples per important pixel faster than the GPU with 8 samples per pixel using multi-sampling anti-aliasing. ## Testable implementation directions

These are engineering inferences from the evidence, not measured Vexel results.

1. **Retain spatially local rendering and bounded caching.** Keep source/vector
   data editable and preserved. Evaluate coarse tile/cell culling and local
   invalidation; measure overlap amplification and cache metadata as well as
   pixels. Compare against the owned CPU renderer before choosing a Metal path.
2. **Include every stage in animation costs.** Measure decoding, path expansion,
   spatial preprocessing, invalidation, rendering and presentation separately
   and together. Use both static pan/zoom and changing artwork/timeline input;
   caching a static illustration cannot establish animated-frame performance.
3. **Separate progress from validation.** A partial preview must not certify an
   unvalidated document. Keep bounded per-step work, cancellation and explicit
   storage errors; charge actual reserved token/table capacity. Streaming
   visitors and retained editable models have different memory requirements.
4. **Measure feedback by task and input.** Record input-to-first-visible-feedback
   and input-to-final-frame for drawing, dragging/nodes, pan/zoom, playback and
   live MCP transactions. Fast previews must converge to faithful output and
   visibly report transaction/progress/cancel state, preserving undo integrity.
5. **Preserve existing product budgets.** ADR0018’s100MB/2second first-content,
   <100ms owner-thread pause and p95<33ms pan/zoom targets remain unchanged.
   Later work orders must name AppleSilicon hardware/OS/build, corpus hashes,
   cold/warm protocol, repeated p50/p95/worst samples and memory/quality results.
   Record end-to-end latency separately from renderer duration. No new broad
   UI/performance suite ran during this research.

## Gaps and next evidence

AppleMetal equivalence, full SVG clips/masks/text/effects, dynamic source editing,
MCP transaction observability and representative-user measurements remain open.
The review does not select an external renderer or retire the owned parser.
Native animation authoring and Rust/AppKit integration still follow the full
product plan. Comprehensive UI/E2E, fidelity, performance, accessibility,
recovery, packaged-release and authentic recorded demos remain final gates.

artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:20:                                                  We study the problem of validating XML documents of size N against general DTDs in the context
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:21:                                              of streaming algorithms. The starting point of this work is a well-known space lower bound. There are
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:22:                                              XML documents and DTDs for which p-pass streaming algorithms require Ω(N/p) space.

artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:28:                                              dently, and we also provide memory efficient streaming algorithms for decoding an XML document given
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:31:                                              external memory can be done with sublinear memory. There is a one-pass algorithm using O( N log N )
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:32:                                              space, and a bidirectional two-pass algorithm using O(log2 N ) space performing this task.
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:36:                                        The area of streaming algorithms has experienced tremendous growth over the last decade in many appli-
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:37:                                        cations. Streaming algorithms sequentially scan the whole input piece by piece in one pass, or in a small
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:38:                                        number of passes (i.e., they do not have random access to the input), while using sublinear memory space,
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:39:                                        ideally polylogarithmic in the size of the input. The design of streaming algorithms is motivated by the ex-
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:40:                                        plosion in the size of the data that algorithms are called upon to process in everyday real-time applications.
artifacts/WO-RUST-RESEARCH-SCIENCE-01/xml-preprint-2010.txt:43:                                        was one of the first applications of this kind of algorithm.

                                                                                            Abstract
                                                  We study the problem of validating XML documents of size N against general DTDs in the context
                                              of streaming algorithms. The starting point of this work is a well-known space lower bound. There are
                                              XML documents and DTDs for which p-pass streaming algorithms require Ω(N/p) space.
                                                  We show that when allowing access to external memory, there is a deterministic streaming algo-
                                              rithm that solves this problem with memory space O(log2 N ), a constant number of auxiliary read/write
                                              streams, and O(log N ) total number of passes on the XML document and auxiliary streams.
                                                  An important intermediate step of this algorithm is the computation of the First-Child-Next-Sibling
                                              (FCNS) encoding of the initial XML document in a streaming fashion. We study this problem indepen-
                                              dently, and we also provide memory efficient streaming algorithms for decoding an XML document given
                                              in its FCNS encoding.
                                                  Furthermore, validating XML documents encoding binary trees in the usual streaming model√ without
                                              external memory can be done with sublinear memory. There is a one-pass algorithm using O( N log N )
                                              space, and a bidirectional two-pass algorithm using O(log2 N ) space performing this task.


                                        1    Introduction
                                        The area of streaming algorithms has experienced tremendous growth over the last decade in many appli-
                                        cations. Streaming algorithms sequentially scan the whole input piece by piece in one pass, or in a small
                                        number of passes (i.e., they do not have random access to the input), while using sublinear memory space,
                                        ideally polylogarithmic in the size of the input. The design of streaming algorithms is motivated by the ex-
                                        plosion in the size of the data that algorithms are called upon to process in everyday real-time applications.
                                        Examples of such applications occur in bioinformatics for genome decoding, in Web databases for the search
                                        of documents, or in network monitoring. The analysis of Internet traffic [1], in which traffic logs are queried,
                                        was one of the first applications of this kind of algorithm.
                                            There are various extensions of this basic streaming model. One of them gives the streaming algorithm
                                        access to an external memory consisting of several read/write streams [9, 11, 7]. Then the streaming algorithm
                                        is also relaxed to perform multiple passes in any direction over the input stream and the auxiliary streams.

 In most of the applications, the number of auxiliary streams is constant and the total number of passes is
logarithmic in the input size.
    Verifying properties or evaluating queries of massive databases is an active and challenging topic. For
relational algebra queries against relational databases, the situation is quite clear. There are bidirectional
O(log N )-pass deterministic streaming algorithms with constant memory space and a constant number of
auxiliary streams [8]. Moreover, the logarithmic number of passes is a necessary condition in order to keep
the memory space sublinear, even if randomization is allowed. The latter was initially stated for one-sided
error [8] and then extended to two-sided error [4, 3].
    In the context of data exchange, especially on the Web, Extended Markup Language (XML) is emerging
as the standard, and is currently drawing much attention in data management research. Only few is known on
XML query processing when only streaming access is allowed to the XML document. For evaluating XQuery
and XPath queries against XML documents of size N , only the lower bound has been extended [8, 4, 3],
meaning that Ω(log N ) passes are necessary. For the upper bound, only simple refinements of the direct
algorithm are known: no auxiliary stream, one pass and linear memory in the height of the XML document,
which in the worst case is as large as N .
    This paper considers the problem of validating XML documents against a given Document Type Definition
(DTD) in a streaming fashion without restrictions on the DTD. Prior works on that topic [18, 17] essentially
try to characterize those DTDs for which validity can be checked by a finite-state automaton, that is a one-
pass deterministic streaming algorithm with constant memory. Concerning arbitrary DTDs, two approaches
have been considered in [18]. The first one leads to an algorithm with memory space linear in the height
of the XML document [18]. The second one consists in constructing a refined DTD of at most quadratic
size, which defines a similar family of tree documents as the original one, and against which validation can
be done with constant space. Nonetheless, for an existing document and DTD, the later requires that both,
documents and DTD, are converted before validation.
    One of the obstacles prior works had to cope with was to check well-formedness of XML documents, that
is every opening tag matches its same-level closing tag. Due to the past work of [14], we can now perform
such a verification with a constant-pass randomized streaming  √ algorithm with sublinear memory space and
no auxiliary streams. In one-pass the memory space is O( N log N ), and collapses to O(log2 N ) with an
additional pass in reverse direction.
    The starting point of this work is the fact that checking validity is hard without auxiliary streams.
There are DTDs defining ternary XML documents for which any p-pass bidirectional randomized streaming
algorithm requires Ω(N/p) space. This lower bound comes from encoding a well known communication
complexity problem, Set-Disjointness, as an XML validity problem. This lower bound should be well-known,
however we are not aware of a complete proof in the literature. In [10], a similar approach using ternary
trees with a reduction to Set-Disjointness is used for proving lower bounds for queries. For the sake of
completeness we provide a proof in Appendix A.
    An XML document is valid against a DTD if for each node, the sequence of the labels of their children
fulfills a regular expression defined in the DTD. For the case of XML documents encoding binary trees,
we present in Section 3 two deterministic streaming algorithms for checking validity with sublinear space.

    "abstract": "Edge aliasing continues to be one of the most prominent problems in real-time graphics, e.g., in games. We present a novel algorithm that uses shared memory between the GPU and the CPU so that these two units can work in concert to solve the edge aliasing problem rapidly. Our system renders the scene as usual on the GPU with one sample per pixel. At the same time, our novel edge aliasing algorithm is executed asynchronously on the CPU. First, a sparse set of important pixels is created. This set may include pixels with geometric silhouette edges, discontinuities in the frame buffer, and pixels/polygons under user-guided artistic control. After that, the CPU runs our sparse rasterizer and fragment shader, which is parallel and SIMD:ified, and directly accesses shared resources (e.g., render targets created by the GPU). Our system can render a scene with shadow mapping with adaptive anti-aliasing with 16 samples per important pixel faster than the GPU with 8 samples per pixel using multi-sampling anti-aliasing. In particular, cloud streaming services, which transmit large amounts of video data and notoriously suffer from low resolution and/or high latency. In addition, display resolutions are growing rapidly, exacerbating the issue. Raster images for large displays prove a significant bottleneck when being transported over communication networks. However the alternative of sending a full 3D scene worth of geometry is even more prohibitive. AGAA reduces aliasing by prefiltering the scene\u2019s sub-pixel geometric detail (foliage, thin railings, etc.) into an aggregate G-buffer that models the distribution of geometry projecting into each pixel. We present Aggregate G-Buffer Anti-Aliasing (AGAA), a new technique for efficient anti-aliased deferred rendering of complex geometry using modern graphics hardware. In geometrically com-plex situations, where many surfaces intersect a pixel, current ren-dering systems shade each contributing surface at least once per pixel. As the sample density and geometric complexity increase, the shading cost becomes prohibitive for real-time rendering. Under deferred shading, so does the required framebuffer memory.     "abstract": "We introduce a novel GPU path rendering method based on scan-line rasterization, which is highly work-efficient but traditionally considered as GPU hostile. Non-boundary pixels are processed in bulk as horizontal spans like in CPU scanline rasterizers, which saves a significant amount of winding number computation workload. The distinction also allows the majority of our algorithmic steps to focus on boundary fragments only, which leads to highly balanced workload among the GPU threads. In addition, we develop a ray shooting pattern that minimizes the global data dependency when computing winding numbers at anti-aliasing samples. This allows us to shift the majority of winding-number-related workload to the same kernel that consumes its result, which saves a significant amount of GPU memory bandwidth.     "abstract": "We present Aggregate G-Buffer Anti-Aliasing (AGAA), a new technique for efficient anti-aliased deferred rendering of complex geometry using modern graphics hardware. In geometrically complex situations, where many surfaces intersect a pixel, current rendering systems shade each contributing surface at least once per pixel. As the sample density and geometric complexity increase, the shading cost becomes prohibitive for real-time rendering. Under deferred shading, so does the required framebuffer memory. AGAA uses the rasterization pipeline to generate a compact, pre-filtered geometric representation inside each pixel. We then shade this at a fixed rate, independent of geometric complexity. By decoupling shading rate from geometric sampling rate, the algorithm reduces the storage and bandwidth costs of a geometry buffer, and allows scaling to high visibility sampling rates for anti-aliasing.     "abstract": "We present a massively parallel vector graphics rendering pipeline that is divided into two components. Tree construction is efficient and parallel at the segment level, enabling dynamic vector graphics. The tree allows efficient random access to the color of individual samples, so the graphics can be warped for special effects. The rendering component processes all samples and pixels in parallel. It was optimized for wide antialiasing filters and a large number of samples per pixel to generate sharp, noise-free images. Our sample scheduler allows pixels with overlapping antialiasing filters to share samples. It groups together samples that can be computed with the same vector operations using little memory or bandwidth. The pipeline is feature-rich, supporting multiple layers of filled paths, each defined by curved outlines (with linear, rational quadratic, and integral cubic B\u00e9zier segments), clipped against other paths, and painted with semi-transparent colors, gradients, or textures. item.text:
**REJECT.** Two documentation defects:

- The report calls the scanline paper “retained as a candidate.” Its PDF fetch failed TLS hostname verification, and only the indexed abstract is saved. That wording could imply a research recommendation from retrieval rank, which the frozen order prohibits. Rephrase it as an abstract-only lead for later primary-source review, with no recommendation.
- The Ng row says “not … application performance,” but the study measures participants’ ability to perceive latency differences during dragging, and the paper discusses performance effects. Clarify that it measures perceptual discrimination in a touch demonstrator; it does not establish Vexel or general application performance.

The checked evidence otherwise supports eight successful, sequential API envelopes; no claim of an exhaustive survey or full reading of every article; the primary PDF access and hardware/preprocessing limits; the XML DTD scope distinction; the participant and just-noticeable-difference caveats; and the related 2020 chapter reconciliation. The report preserves existing budgets and avoids claims of Apple Metal performance, a best algorithm, adoption, or feature completion. No private query input, new dependency, GPL source, or application tests were found in the reviewed material. No edits, network access, installs, tests, or builds were performed.
